newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST - HK Newspaper Headlines - Dec 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - HK Newspaper Headlines - Dec 27.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- Hong Kong's Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa will try to meet the chief of the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) Michael Leung next week to ask why he is planning to leave his post.
-- Up to 20 small local brokers have agreed to merge their businesses in a bid to cut costs and offset increasing competition from large international brokerages.
-- China's actual foreign direct investment was expected to increase to more than US$40 billion this year.
-- China Eastern Airlines' share flotation is seen happening in late February at the earliest.

-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- Chief Secretary Anson Chan, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang and several other top civil servants could be asked to quit within a year of the handover next June 30 if they do not meet expectations, Preparatory Committee sources say.
-- More than 10 million pirated compact discs were seized in China in 1996 and 140 people arrested for copyright breaches.

-- ECONOMIC JOURNAL -- Wharf Cable is projected to post an operating loss of around HK$400 million in 1996 but the loss is seen falling to below HK$200 million in 1997, with a return to profits expected in 1998.
-- WEN WEI PO -- Beijing clarified that the position and function of its Taiwan Affairs Office had not changed as some Hong Kong media had reported.
-- Shenzhen would start to treat foreign investors, employees and enterprises the same way as Chinese nationals next year.
-- APPLE DAILY -- Concord Pacific Holdings Ltd plans to take a stake in Canadian-listed Burcon International Development Inc, controlled by Tak Cheung and Hutchison Whampoa Ltd.

-- MING PAO -- Prices of flight tickets from Canada, Australia, Britain and the United States -- homes to the majority of Hong Kong emigrants -- would be increased by 10 to 20 percent for the six-week period before the handover.
